title: ABAIR's Irish synthetic voices power an NVDA screenreader plugin for visually impaired pupils, 'extensively tested with visually-impaired school children'
summary: SLPAT 2022 paper by the ABAIR team (Trinity College Dublin): Irish NVDA plugin with Braille output, NCBI-funded, built with a blind researcher, tested with visually impaired pupils; no dated outcome.
account: Ní Chasaide, Barnes, Ní Chiaráin, McGuirk, Morrin, Nic Corcráin and Cummins of the ABAIR initiative described, at the Ninth Workshop on Speech and Language Processing for Assistive Technologies (SLPAT-2022, 27 May 2022, the date used here), three assistive applications of ABAIR's Irish speech technology, the first being 'A screenreading facility for Irish has been developed as a plugin for the NVDA screenreader, prompted by urgent pleas from parents and grandparents of visually impaired children in the Gaeltacht or attending Irish-medium schools', for whom only three books existed in Irish Braille. 'With funding from the National Council for the Blind in Ireland (NCBI) a blind researcher worked with the ABAIR team to develop the NVDA screenreader plugin', which adds Braille output through the Liblouis translator and lets users choose a male or female voice and the reading speed. The paper states 'The system was extensively tested with visually-impaired school children and a full technical description is available in McGuirk (2005)' (the reference list gives McGuirk 2015, an M.Phil. dissertation). It names no child, school, date or measured result, and describes the voices as text-to-speech synthesis without stating the synthesis method. No source independent of the developers was found in this pass.
purpose: Built so that blind and visually impaired pupils can hear and read Irish text through a screenreader with Braille output; use by school children was that intended purpose.
system: ABAIR Irish-language synthetic voices (abair.ie) delivered through an NVDA screenreader plugin with Liblouis Braille output
developer: ABAIR project, Phonetics and Speech Laboratory, Trinity College Dublin (Ní Chasaide et al.), with a blind researcher funded by the National Council for the Blind of Ireland
deployer: Visually impaired pupils in Gaeltacht and Irish-medium schools, per the paper
domain: Accessibility / assistive technology for an endangered language
segment: Blind and low-vision school pupils learning through Irish
taxonomy_note: Accessibility is the direct fit. General benefit with null depths: the developers' peer-reviewed workshop paper reports that the plugin was built and extensively tested with visually impaired school children but gives no identifiable child, date or outcome, and it is the only fetched source; it does not say whether the synthesis is neural, so the AI character rests on it being a text-to-speech system from a speech-technology research group.

ratings.reason: The paper reports extensive testing with visually impaired school children and the motivating need (three Irish Braille books), but no identified pupil, date or measured gain.
Access to written Irish for the 4,701 school-age blind or visually impaired people cited from the 2016 census is the stated aim; no uptake figure is given.

ai_role.statement: Only the developers' own account could be fetched: the ABAIR team's SLPAT 2022 paper says the Irish NVDA plugin with their synthetic voices was built with a blind researcher and extensively tested with visually impaired school children, without any outcome data. The paper does not describe the synthesis method, so neither the system's AI character nor its contribution to any pupil's reading can be assessed from fetched sources.
